description: How businesses set prices and promote products to compete in changing markets.
content_html:
Pricing in a Competitive Market

Setting the right price is one of the most consequential decisions a business makes. Price must cover costs, generate profit and reflect what customers are willing to pay — all at the same time. There is no single correct strategy. Instead, businesses choose between several approaches depending on the competitive landscape, the product’s position in its life cycle, the market segment they are targeting and the technology available.

Competitive pricing means setting prices in line with rivals. It is common in markets where products are similar and customers can easily compare, such as petrol stations, supermarket own-brand goods, or budget airlines. The risk is that competing purely on price can reduce profit margins for every firm in the market. A business using this strategy must keep costs tightly controlled to remain profitable.

Price skimming involves charging a premium price at launch and then gradually lowering the price over time. It works best for innovative or high-demand products where early adopters are willing to pay a premium to be first — new games consoles, flagship smartphones and luxury goods often use this approach. As the product matures and competition increases, the price falls to reach a wider market.

Penetration pricing does the opposite: a new product enters the market at a low price to attract customers quickly and build market share. The business accepts lower profit margins in the short term in exchange for volume. Once customers are loyal, the price may be raised. Streaming services and budget gyms have used this tactic successfully, though the risk is that customers may leave if the price rises too steeply.

Key Fact

The four main pricing strategies are competitive pricing (match rivals), price skimming (high at launch, then fall), penetration pricing (low at launch to build share) and psychological pricing (e.g. £9.99 instead of £10.00). Technology, competition, market segments and the product life cycle all influence which strategy works best.

Influences on Pricing Strategy

No pricing decision exists in isolation. Technology affects pricing because online price-comparison websites mean customers can instantly see if a business is overcharging, making competitive pricing more important than ever. The stage of the product life cycle matters: a new product with no competition can sustain a skimming price, while a declining product may need deep discounts to clear stock. Market segments differ in price sensitivity — a premium segment will pay more for quality or exclusivity, while a mass-market segment responds to value for money.

A market segment is a distinct group within a larger market. Different segments have very different attitudes to price. A ‘budget’ segment is highly price-sensitive: a small price increase leads to a large drop in sales. A ‘premium’ segment is less price-sensitive because customers associate higher prices with better quality. Businesses that understand their segment can set prices with confidence, rather than guessing.

Promotion Strategies

Promotion is how a business communicates with potential customers. The goal is to raise awareness, build desire and convert that desire into a sale. Different promotional tools suit different markets, budgets and objectives.

Advertising uses paid media — television, radio, print, online display — to reach a broad audience. It is expensive but can build brand awareness quickly. Sponsorship links a brand to an event, team or individual to improve its image. Product trials (free samples or demonstrations) allow customers to experience the product before buying, reducing perceived risk. Special offers such as discounts, “buy one get one free” deals or loyalty cards incentivise immediate purchase and can shift stock quickly. Branding builds long-term recognition and trust through consistent use of a name, logo and values.

Key Fact

Promotion strategies include advertising, sponsorship, product trials, special offers and branding. Each suits different market segments and budgets. No single approach is best for every product — the most effective businesses choose a promotional mix that matches their target audience and objectives.

Technology and Promotion

Technology has transformed how businesses promote their products. Targeted advertising online allows businesses to reach specific segments with precision — a fitness brand can show adverts only to users who have recently searched for gym memberships. This reduces wasted spend and improves the return on the promotional budget.

Viral advertising via social media is a low-cost but unpredictable approach. A clever video or post can be shared millions of times at no extra cost to the business, generating enormous brand awareness. The challenge is that virality cannot be guaranteed — many planned ‘viral’ campaigns fail to spread beyond a small audience. E-newsletters allow direct communication with existing customers, delivering personalised offers and updates to people who have already shown interest in the brand.

Students sometimes treat “promotion” and “advertising” as the same thing. They are not. Advertising is one type of promotional activity — it involves paid media. Promotion is the broader category that also includes sponsorship, product trials, special offers, branding, viral social media content, e-newsletters and personal selling. In a business exam answer, if you are asked about promotional strategies, you should discuss the full range, not just advertising.
exam_tip_html: For a 6-mark Analyse question on pricing or promotion, the question will give you a business context. Use it — state a specific detail from the scenario (a product, a price, a customer type) in your first sentence, then build your analysis around it. A generic answer that could apply to any business will stall in the Developing tier. For a 9-mark Discuss question on promotion, examiners want you to explore both sides: the advantages of a strategy and the reasons why it might not work for this business. End with a supported judgement rather than a neutral summary. Remember: on any calculation question, the final numerical answer (with correct units — £ or %) is what earns marks. Show your working but make the answer unmissable.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Pricing strategies include competitive pricing, price skimming, penetration pricing and psychological pricing. The right choice depends on competition, market segment, the product life cycle stage and technology.
  • Promotion tools include advertising, sponsorship, product trials, special offers and branding. Technology adds targeted online advertising, viral social media campaigns and e-newsletters to the mix.
  • Promotion is the broad category; advertising is one tool within it. Businesses choose a promotional mix that matches their target audience, budget and objectives.

practice_questions.marks: Launching a product at a low price to gain market share quickly before raising the price later. [1 mark — accept any accurate definition that captures the low-launch-price and market-share objective]

practice_questions.text: Harbour & Bloom is a small artisan candle business in Truro. It sells a standard candle for £12.00. It wants to try psychological pricing on a new premium range. Calculate the psychological price Harbour & Bloom should charge if the full price of the premium candle is £20.00.
practice_questions.marks:
Formula: psychological price = full price minus a small amount, typically ending in .99 or .95 (1 mark for method)
Answer: £19.99 (1 mark for correct answer with £ sign)
[2 marks for £19.99 only; 1 mark if method is shown but the answer is incomplete or missing the £ sign. Note: £19.95 is also acceptable. No marks for £20.00 unchanged.]

practice_questions.text: Harbour & Bloom is considering two promotional strategies: sponsoring a local craft fair (£500 cost) or running targeted advertising on social media (£500 budget). Outline one benefit of using targeted online advertising for Harbour & Bloom.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for a benefit with development and context:
• Targeted online advertising allows Harbour & Bloom to reach users who have already shown interest in gifts or candles (1 mark), meaning the £500 budget is spent only on people likely to buy (1 mark), which improves the return on promotion spend compared with sponsoring a general craft fair where many visitors may have no interest in candles (1 mark).
[1 mark for a relevant benefit, 1 mark for development, 1 mark for a contextual link to the scenario]

practice_questions.text:
Analyse how the stage of the product life cycle can influence a business's choice of pricing strategy.

Paragon Robotics Ltd has launched an innovative domestic cleaning robot priced at £899. It is the only product of its type currently on the market.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Identifies that Paragon Robotics is in the introduction phase and correctly connects this to a skimming strategy with at least two well-developed analytical points. Uses specific contextual detail (£899 price, no competition, innovative product) throughout. Analysis shows awareness that the strategy must change as competitors enter.

Secure (3–4 marks): Correctly identifies the life cycle phase and links it to a pricing strategy. Some use of context. The response reads as analytical rather than purely descriptive.

Developing (2 marks): Describes a pricing strategy or life cycle phase correctly but the analytical link between them is limited. Context from the source may be absent.

Emerging (1 mark): Basic recall of a pricing strategy or life cycle phase with no analytical development.

practice_questions.text: Zephyr Active is a mid-sized UK sportswear brand. Its main product range has been in maturity for two years. A new direct-to-consumer competitor has recently entered the market with lower prices. Discuss whether Zephyr Active should respond by reducing its prices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Two or more well-developed analytical points on both sides (reasons to cut price and reasons not to). Specific contextual details (maturity phase, new low-price competitor, brand position) are embedded throughout, not added as decoration. The conclusion is supported and adds a new evaluative point — for example, that the decision depends on whether Zephyr’s customers are price-sensitive or brand-loyal.

Secure (5–7 marks): Both sides addressed with some analytical development and use of context. The conclusion is present but may not add new evaluative thinking beyond what was already said.

Developing (3–4 marks): One side discussed with some development, or both sides described superficially without genuine analysis. Limited use of the scenario details.

Emerging (1–2 marks): A basic statement of preference or a generic description of price strategy with no analytical content.

practice_questions.text:
Zephyr Active is deciding between two promotional approaches to respond to its new competitor:
Option A: Invest £80,000 in a television advertising campaign to reinforce brand awareness.
Option B: Launch a targeted social media campaign and influencer partnership for £30,000.

Justify which promotional strategy you would recommend to Zephyr Active.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): A clear recommendation is made and fully developed using the specific context (maturity phase, new competitor, budget contrast of £80k vs £30k, brand position). The student shows awareness of the trade-offs (reach vs precision, brand building vs sales activation) and explains why the chosen option’s advantages outweigh its drawbacks in this context. The conclusion adds a new evaluative point (e.g. long-term brand equity vs short-term market share defence).

Secure (7–9 marks): A clear recommendation with developed reasoning using some contextual detail. The student acknowledges at least one drawback of the chosen option. The conclusion is present but may restate earlier arguments rather than adding new evaluation.

Developing (4–6 marks): A preference is stated with some reasoning. Both options may be described in parallel without a clear recommendation. Contextual detail is used superficially.

Emerging (1–3 marks): A preference is stated with limited or generic reasoning. No meaningful engagement with the contextual details.

Which of the following is an example of using technology in promotion?
options: Placing an advert in a local newspaper
Sending targeted adverts to users based on their online browsing history
Offering a buy-one-get-one-free deal in a physical store

knowledge_checks.q: Charging a similar price to competitors so price is not the deciding factor for customers is called _____ pricing.
Promotional content that spreads rapidly because users share it across social media networks is known as _____ advertising.
Match each promotional tool to its key feature:
right: Links the brand to an event or individual to improve its image
Allows customers to experience the product before buying, reducing perceived risk
Discounts or bundle deals that incentivise an immediate purchase

flashcard_questions.a: Setting prices in line with rivals so that price is not the deciding factor for customers.
Launching at a high price to maximise revenue from early customers, then reducing the price over time.
Launching at a low price to gain market share quickly, then raising the price once customers are loyal.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of psychological pricing.
flashcard_questions.a: Charging £9.99 instead of £10.00 to make the price feel lower.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two factors that influence a business's choice of pricing strategy.
flashcard_questions.a: Competition and market segment (also accept: product life cycle stage, technology).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between promotion and advertising?
flashcard_questions.a: Advertising is one type of promotion; promotion also includes sponsorship, trials, offers and branding.
Using data about a user's browsing behaviour to show them adverts relevant to what they are likely to buy.
Promotional content spread rapidly by users sharing it on social media at low cost to the business.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might a business in the introduction phase of the product life cycle use price skimming?
flashcard_questions.a: There is no competition yet, so early adopters will pay a premium for the new product.
A group of customers who share similar characteristics and respond similarly to a product or marketing message.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does competitive pricing require tight cost control?
flashcard_questions.a: Matching rivals' prices leaves little room to raise prices, so profit depends on keeping costs low.

flashcard_questions.q: What is branding as a promotional strategy?
flashcard_questions.a: Building long-term recognition and trust through consistent use of a name, logo and values.

glossary_terms.definition: Charging a similar price to competitors so that price is not the deciding factor for customers.
Launching a product at a high price to maximise revenue from early customers before reducing it.
Launching a product at a low price to gain a large market share quickly before raising the price later.
A group of customers who share similar characteristics and respond similarly to a product or marketing message.
Using data about a user's online behaviour, location and interests to show them relevant advertisements.
Promotional content spread rapidly by users sharing it across social media networks, achieving wide reach at low cost.
